article.articleSummary:
- Anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) outbreaks are killing hippos in Democratic Republic of the Congo's Virunga National Park, with lab confirmation of approximately 30 hippo deaths within a month. No human infections reported in the current outbreak as of 2026-11-05, but authorities warn that handling infected carcasses, skinning, or consuming contaminated meat could transmit the disease. March 2025 saw a more severe spillover, with about 65 hippos killed in Virunga and 15 human infections in neighboring Uganda, including two deaths. Anthrax spores can persist in soil for decades; drought drives wildlife to scarce water sources, heightening exposure. - Cholera outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has reached severe levels, with WHO reporting about 1,800 deaths and nearly 60,000 cases since the start of the year (as of Nov 4). The DRC is concurrently contending the largest Ebola outbreak to date, creating a critical health emergency. Most cholera cases are in the eastern provinces of North Kivu and South Kivu, regions contested by armed groups including the M23, with concerns about spread along the Congo River basin toward Kinshasa. Ongoing insecurity and remote outbreaks hinder surveillance, patient access, and delivery of supplies. The rainy season could worsen transmission, given sanitation and water challenges. The policy targets US-bound passengers and represents an added border-control measure in response to the outbreak in Central Africa.

Zoonoses teams intensify home visits to remove breeding sites and educate residents. In Sorocaba, dengue cases fell from 14,130 (Jan–Oct 2025) to 81 (Jan–Oct 2026). - Brazil may see a 20-40% rise in dengue cases in 2027 due to El Niño impacts and ongoing dengue transmission, with chikungunya risk rising as well. The forecast incorporates El Niño effects and the dengue serotype dynamics after a two-year decline left more people susceptible. Fiocruz projects about 1.5 million probable dengue cases in 2027 without El Niño; under a strong El Niño, increases are projected across all regions (South +138.2%, Central-West +98.4%, Southeast +84.9%, North +68.9%, Northeast +49.1%). - Brazil's Ministry of Health warns that El Niño–driven climate changes are likely to increase dengue and chikungunya in 2027. The projection underscores heightened arbovirus risk linked to climate variability, with potential regional impacts across Brazil. Health Minister Alexandre Padilha says he intends to resume the dengue vaccine developed by Instituto Butantan, which was suspended in June after reports of severe adverse reactions. Padilha emphasized that safety analyses are still pending and he did not provide a timeline for deciding whether to reinstate the Butantan-DV vaccine in Brazil’s public health system (SUS, Sistema Único de Saúde). article.articleHeadline: The World Health Organization approved clinical trials of two new vaccines developed against Bundibugyo virus.
article.articleSummary:
- WHO has, as of 4 November 2026, approved clinical trials for two new vaccines against Bundibugyo virus, the Ebola virus species involved in a current Ebola outbreak. One vaccine was developed by Oxford University in collaboration with Serum Institute of India; the other by Moderna. The approval enables initiating human trials to assess safety, immunogenicity, and preliminary efficacy; trial specifics such as design, populations, endpoints, and timelines are not detailed. The move reflects international collaboration to broaden preventive options against Bundibugyo virus–related outbreaks and to diversify vaccine platforms amid ongoing Ebola activity. This development highlights vaccine development efforts against distinct Ebola virus species.

Ervebo, licensed for the Zaire ebolavirus strain, is already used in trials but not for Bundibugyo. The two additional candidates would be included in these trials: ChAdOx1, an adenovirus-vectored vaccine developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India; and a Moderna mRNA vaccine. - On 4 November 2026, WHO experts urged adding two Ebola vaccines to ongoing clinical trials: the ChAdOx1 vaccine from the University of Oxford in collaboration with the Serum Institute of India, and Moderna’s mRNA-1469. To curb the rising mosquito population, a meeting of vector-control experts—led by Chief Pest Control Officer Selvakumar and attended by about 20 specialists—was held to tighten measures against mosquito breeding in rainwater drains. Concurrent medical camps were organized in Chennai’s Thiru Vi Ka Nagar zone and adjacent areas to prevent dengue-like febrile illnesses during the monsoon. - As of October 30, 2026, dengue fever has been confirmed in 13,108 people across the state, with 44 deaths attributed to dengue and a rising number of people seeking treatment for dengue-like symptoms, including in Kottayam district. The year 2026 surpasses 2025, which had 10,909 confirmed cases. Suspected dengue cases reached 35,192 by Oct 30, 2026, up from 29,060 in 2025, with suspected dengue deaths at 35 this year (versus 6 last year). Given ongoing rainfall, the public should eliminate stagnant water and promptly seek care at health facilities for fever or dengue-like symptoms rather than self-treat.

article.articleHeadline: Over 700 experts will attend the Dengue Fever Conference 2026, promoting the application of science in disease prevention and control.
article.articleSummary: Dengue fever remains a global public health challenge, including Vietnam, with transmission shaped by climate change and urbanization. The Dengue Summit 2026 in Hanoi on 5–6 November 2026 will host nearly 700 delegates from domestic and international health sectors, including representatives from 34 provincial health departments. The two-day event, organized by Vietnam’s Ministry of Health’s Department of Prevention with Hanoi Medical University and Takeda Vietnam, aims to promote science-based applications, research, and technical exchanges to strengthen dengue prevention, surveillance, vector control, diagnosis, treatment, and outbreak response nationwide. Sessions cover epidemiology, updated treatment guidelines, data sharing, and digital surveillance with early warning, plus risk communication and policy integration. International speakers include Rosana Richtmann (Brazil) on proactive dengue prevention in Brazil’s Expanded Immunization Program; Jarir At Thobari (Indonesia) on integrating health-technology evidence into policy; and Shane Fairlie (WHO) on risk-based communication. Over 60 domestic posters will be presented at Lotte Hanoi Hotel.

article.articleHeadline: KEMRI joins global Dengue research alliance
article.articleSummary: Kenya becomes the first African country to join the Dengue Alliance, established in 2022, to advance safe, effective dengue treatments and strengthen research, surveillance, diagnostics and clinical management. Kenya's membership will expand collaboration and ensure African patients are considered in future clinical studies. WHO data show about 10,000 dengue cases in Kenya from January to August 2026, up from 4,300 in 2025 and 1,400 in 2024, with all four dengue virus serotypes detected since the first outbreak in 1982. Transmission has extended beyond coastal areas into northern and western Kenya and near borders with Uganda, South Sudan and Ethiopia. While vaccines and vector-control have advanced, no specific dengue treatment exists. A DNDi–Serum Institute of India candidate is slated for Phase III in early 2027 (Brazil, Thailand, Malaysia). DNDi-led studies in Senegal, Ghana and DRC underscore underdiagnosis and underreporting, guiding new medicines development; KEMRI will contribute arboviral research and climate-health expertise.

article.articleHeadline: Veterinarians warn of an increase in leptospirosis cases in dogs in Londrina.
article.articleSummary: Leptospirosis cases in dogs are rising in Londrina, Brazil, with a veterinary clinic reporting weekly consultations for three to four months; no official data yet. Leptospirosis is a bacterial zoonosis transmitted mainly through rodent urine, with the rainy season increasing environmental risk as the bacterium can persist six months to a year. Exposure is outdoor dog food and water bowls left overnight, attracting rodents. Prevention centers on canine vaccination included in the Dectuple vaccine, protecting four leptospira serovars; owners should remove bowls after meals and monitor for apathy, loss of appetite, and vomiting. In advanced cases, jaundice, muscle stiffness, and sepsis may occur; treatment uses antibiotics and, if severe, IV therapy. Humans can acquire the infection from animal urine or contaminated environments; cats less often affected, and there are no vaccines for cats or humans. Keep dogs up to date on vaccination and seek care for suspected infection.

Scabies is a skin infection caused by the Sarcoptes scabiei mite, primarily spread through direct skin-to-skin contact. Symptoms include intense itching, especially at night, and skin lesions on the wrists, between the fingers, armpits, waist, buttocks, and genital area, often with scratching. Authorities urge individuals with symptoms to seek evaluation at Basic Health Units (UBS) and follow prescribed treatment. Ongoing monitoring continues; reporting isolated cases does not constitute an epidemiological outbreak.

article.articleHeadline: Informative lecture on preventing symptomatic anthrax for rural producers.
article.articleSummary: Symptomatic blackleg (Clostridium chauvoei) in cattle was the focus of a 20 October preventive briefing in Mogi das Cruzes, Brazil, organized by the Municipal Secretariat of Agriculture and Food Security with students from Centro Universitário Braz Cubas. The session highlighted rapid disease progression and high mortality, listing signs such as muscular swelling (especially in the thighs and neck), high fever, depression, lethargy, and crepitation from gas in tissues, with death typically within 12–48 hours of onset. Producers were warned not to confuse symptomatic blackleg with anthrax (carbúnculo hemático) and to avoid carcass necropsy to prevent environmental and human contamination by spores. Preventive measures emphasized include strict vaccination schedules, proper carcass disposal per sanitary and environmental norms, and ongoing herd biosafety and surveillance. If signs appear, immediate veterinary evaluation is essential.

article.articleHeadline: Bedridden woman for ten years with a nonhealing pressure ulcer found to be caused by latent tuberculosis; Traditional Chinese Medicine intangible heritage therapy relieves the chronic illness.
article.articleSummary: A fifty-something bedridden woman from Taizhou developed a nonhealing left hip pressure ulcer, following paralysis caused by a psoas abscess. Weeks of standard wound care failed, and a wound culture at Nanjing Integrated Traditional Chinese and Western Medicine Hospital’s Wound Clinic revealed Mycobacterium tuberculosis in the exudate, identifying a tuberculous pressure ulcer—rare and treatment-challenging. After diagnosis, clinicians implemented a combined approach: systemic anti-tuberculosis therapy to control infection, surgical debridement of the ulcer, and Xu’s Ulcer Therapy (a traditional Chinese medicine external application and dressing method) to promote granulation. The ulcer rapidly improved, exudate decreased, and healthy tissue formed, leading to complete healing and discharge. The case highlights that pressure ulcers in long-term bedridden patients can harbor uncommon infections and should be evaluated at experienced centers if healing remains stalled beyond one month.

article.articleHeadline: Once infected, you’ll be a lifelong carrier! This virus is entering a period of high incidence.
article.articleSummary: Shingles (herpes zoster), caused by reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus, is entering a high-incidence period in autumn–winter in Jingzhou, Hubei Province, China. After primary infection (chickenpox), the virus remains latent in dorsal root ganglia and can reactivate to cause painful vesicular rashes along nerve distributions. Lesions are not confined to the waist; they can affect the head, neck, chest, eyes, ears, and sometimes the face. Transmission occurs via the live virus in vesicle fluid; while most adults have prior VZV exposure, unvaccinated children should avoid direct contact with active lesions. Prompt antiviral treatment within 72 hours of rash onset, adequate dosing, and analgesia are essential to limit nerve damage and reduce postherpetic neuralgia. Vaccination markedly lowers incidence and complications, and immune health—regular sleep, moderate exercise, and chronic disease management (e.g., diabetes, COPD)—helps prevention. Source: National Emergency Broadcast, Jingzhou Media Center.

In March 2025, a U.S. court awarded Missouri about $24.5 billion after Chinese defendants did not appear; China rejects the allegations and seeks to overturn the ruling.

article.articleHeadline: Sixty-something man admitted to ICU after an outdoor outing; was a tiny cut while washing his hands the culprit? Doctors warn to beware "hookworm disease".
article.articleSummary: Leptospira infection (leptospirosis) in Chengdu, Sichuan, China, hospitalized elderly woman after outdoor family outing. She developed high fever, severe fatigue, calf pain, and decreased urine; condition rapidly worsened with infection-related organ dysfunction and septic shock, leading to ICU admission. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of clinical samples rapidly confirmed Leptospira as the causative pathogen. The exposure likely occurred when she sustained a minor skin puncture washing hands at an outdoor pond with contaminated water/soil from rodents. With sensitive antibiotics and multidisciplinary management, she recovered and was discharged. The disease is zoonotic, with rodents and pigs as reservoirs; emphasize prevention: avoid contact with stagnant water after rain, wear waterproof boots and gloves when wading or cleaning mud, cover wounds, and reduce exposure to animal urine.

article.articleHeadline: The waterless health center that fights Ebola, cholera, measles, and mpox in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
article.articleSummary: South Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Lugendo health center is grappling with Ebola, cholera, measles, and mpox under war conditions. Médecins du Monde notes that the facility depends on a weekly water turn, leaving staff unable to perform basic hygiene or prepare cholera rehydration solutions when water runs out. A recent cholera surge left four inpatients needing fluids, and the team had to deliver 300 liters of water with borrowed jugs to maintain care. The Ebola outbreak in the DRC is the deadliest on record there, with over 10,400 confirmed cases and more than 5,100 deaths; measles and malaria also strain the system. The program emphasizes triage, early detection, isolation, handwashing, cleaning, and chlorination, but water access remains a bottleneck. Plans include adding a 5,000-liter tank to the center’s 500-liter depot, plus a second 5,000-liter rainwater tank, and expanding community chlorine points, to ensure continuous service and longer-term resilience.

article.articleHeadline: Congo-Kinshasa: Ebola Spreads to Eighth DRC Province As WFP Delivers Food, Builds Treatment Centres and Keeps Supplies Moving
article.articleSummary: As of 4 November 2026, Ebola has spread to the eighth province of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). WFP coordinates food and logistics to support patients, families and health teams amid insecurity and poor roads. The six‑month plan provides dry rations for over 500,000 relatives and hot meals for affected households. WFP has delivered 744,000 hot meals in 59 facilities and moved over 3,000 metric tons of food to families. UNHAS has flown 1,255 flights, carrying 10,272 responders and 483 metric tons of cargo. The Logistics Cluster runs bases in Isiro and across Ituri and Haut‑Uélé, storing 3,417 metric tons for 43 partners and delivering 2,653 metric tons by air/road. Musienene hosts the first ETC; Bunia’s is under construction; four more ETCs, including one in Goma, are planned. WFP seeks USD 214 million, including USD 78.6 million for meals. Challenges: insecurity, roads, weather; funding needed to sustain containment.

article.articleHeadline: DRC: North Kivu - IRC strengthens the capacity of community actors to better protect populations affected by Ebola.
article.articleSummary: Two-day training in Butembo for about 30 community actors and health professionals aims to bolster protection of vulnerable groups—women, children, and families affected by Ebola—in North Kivu, DRC. Ebola virus disease brings health risks plus stigma, violence, abuse, and psychological distress. Trainees will identify vulnerabilities, provide initial psychosocial support, and refer cases to appropriate services while safeguarding confidentiality. IRC says the initiative makes the response safer and more humane by helping responders detect distress and risks of violence or exploitation and offer immediate support. Participants will be better prepared to address gender-based violence, child protection, and abuse within the Ebola response in the Grand North, and to engage communities to ease concerns and mistrust of Ebola treatment centers. Survivors and affected families will receive improved support from more trained staff handling sensitive information. Funded by Irish Aid.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola: Community Investigations Help Ituri Respond to Death-Related Alerts - ACP
article.articleSummary: Ebola virus disease in Ituri's Nizi health zone, Democratic Republic of the Congo, prompts community-led investigations that inform response. From August 10–18, 2026, with WHO support, four health areas were surveyed to identify social and cultural drivers of resistance to Ebola interventions and to address community deaths. Findings highlighted practices facilitating transmission: self-medication, reliance on traditional healers, home-based care, and handling bodies during funeral rites, prompting adapted risk communication. Following the assessment, local leaders, religious figures, and community authorities led sensitization sessions to promote preventive behaviors and safer burials. Nizi had 827 confirmed cases and 488 deaths by July 2026, with 59% of deaths occurring in the community; in October, 119 confirmed cases and 51 community deaths were reported. Families are urged to report deaths promptly, limit contact with corpses, and refer suspected cases to care facilities to interrupt transmission; WHO supports culturally tailored prevention strategies.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in Ituri: Community Engagement, a Key Factor in the Response (Dr. Michel Muvudi) - ACP.
article.articleSummary: On 4 November 2026 in Bunia, Ituri, northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, the endgame of the 17th Ebola virus disease outbreak hinges on community engagement, according to a World Bank specialist. Dr. Michel Muvudi told a community forum that success in interrupting transmission requires local leaders and residents to co-create risk messages and tailor response measures to fit local realities. He stressed that communities, directly bearing the epidemic's impact, should be partners rather than passive recipients, capable of identifying what to do and what to avoid. The discussion included chiefs of Bahema Banywagi and Bahema d'Irumu, a civil-society vice-coordinator for Ituri, and community relay agents. The emphasis on locally owned communication and partnerships highlights a pathway to reduce transmission and bring the outbreak to a close.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in Isiro: the vice-governor calls for vigilance and patriotism. - ACP.
article.articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in Isiro, capital of Haut-Uele province, northeast DRC, prompted a public appeal by Vice-Governor Christophe Dara Matata to bolster vigilance and patriotism. During a weekly prayer at the Maranatha Catholic Charismatic community center in Isiro, officials urged strict adherence to barrier measures to end the Ebola epidemic and prevent further transmission. Matata called on believers to act as health ambassadors within families and neighborhoods, countering misinformation that could undermine response efforts. The vice-governor also addressed political and security concerns, condemning attempts to seize power by force, and urged prayers for the nation, President Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi Tshilombo, provincial authorities, and lasting peace. The message emphasizes community mobilization, accurate information, and adherence to prevention measures as key to overcoming Ebola in the region.

article.articleHeadline: DRC: Fwamba announces $771 million from the IMF in December, of which $240 is for the Ebola response.
article.articleSummary: DRC secures IMF accord on the fourth ECF review and the third RSF review, with an expected December disbursement of about $771 million, including roughly $240 million for the Ebola response (2026 phase). IMF board review is planned mid-December; the mission (Oct 22–Nov 4) was led by Calixte Ahokpossi. The IMF cites three shocks—conflict in the East, resurgence of Ebola, and the Middle East war—and urges prudent, coordinated fiscal and monetary policy and accelerated reforms to preserve macro stability and inclusive growth. Kinshasa requests higher 2026–27 deficit ceilings and increased access to both the ECF (to cover Ebola costs and external financing needs) and the RSF (to cushion macro-budget risks from health shocks). The IMF notes earlier deficit ceiling miss and ongoing execution risks (revenue measures, wage bill control, prioritization). Inflation is projected near 9% by end-2026 due to higher oil prices; the December Board review will consider the requests.

Officials launched barangay-level interventions, including health education drives in schools and residences, and deployed Barangay Health Workers for household monitoring. City Health Office teams distributed medical kits (permethrin, cetirizine, paracetamol, multivitamins, sulfur soap) and instructed families on home isolation and sanitation. Health officials remind scabies spreads via prolonged skin-to-skin contact or shared bedding/clothing; early evaluation and hygiene remain key.

article.articleHeadline: Theatres and factories in Nagai have become breeding grounds for dengue mosquitoes: Health Department imposes Rs. 11,500 fine.
article.articleSummary: Nagapattinam, Tamil Nadu faces dengue risk after health officials found Aedes mosquito larvae breeding in stagnant water inside a private cinema theatre, an ice plant, several factories, and a lathe workshop within Nagapattinam Municipality. Under the Tamil Nadu Public Health Act 1939, authorities levied a total fine of Rs 11,500: cinema Rs 5,000; ice plant Rs 5,000; factory Rs 1,000; lathe workshop Rs 500. Aedes, the dengue vector, is described as biting during the day. Preventive actions include removing standing water, cleaning waste such as old tires and plastic containers, covering water storage tanks, and maintaining clean surroundings. Dengue prevention and awareness drives are being intensified in Nagapattinam, with warnings of further action if violations persist. The investigation underscores shared responsibility of businesses and the public to maintain hygiene to curb dengue transmission.

article.articleSummary: HIV infection alert in Ranchi, Jharkhand, India, with 173 new HIV-positive cases detected among 23,887 people tested from April to October 2026; Jharkhand-wide 1,139 new infections identified in 147,639 tests, with 1,095 people linked to anti-retroviral therapy (ART), yielding about 96% treatment linkage. article.articleHeadline: Assam: Over 50 students at engineering college fall ill, dead monkey found in water tank
article.articleSummary: In Guwahati, Assam, 52 students from Hostel 7 at Assam Engineering College fell ill after using water from a tank in which a dead monkey was found, prompting foul-smelling water concerns. The college cleaned the tank and moved the mess to another hostel; classes resumed. No deaths were reported. The campus lies near a hill with a large monkey population, contributing to safety concerns and a recent rabies vaccination for a bitten student. The administration has alerted the forest department about the monkey menace.

article.articleHeadline: Dangerous tropical virus transmitted in Switzerland for the first time.
article.articleSummary: Chikungunya virus has been locally transmitted for the first time in Ticino, Switzerland, with affected individuals reporting no recent travel to endemic areas. Transmission occurred via Aedes mosquitoes, including the Asian tiger mosquito, now established in parts of Switzerland. Classic symptoms are sudden high fever and severe joint and muscle pain, sometimes with headaches and a rash; onset typically 7–9 days after a bite. Although usually not life-threatening, joint pain and fatigue can persist for weeks or months. Chikungunya is common in tropical and subtropical regions, notably Africa, India, Southeast Asia, the Caribbean, and Central/South America. Europe has seen local outbreaks in Italy and France. Transmission requires infected mosquitoes and suitable climate; Switzerland had previously been considered to have very low risk.

article.articleHeadline: Health department alert amid the threat of floods and cyclones, nine-point directives issued to CMHO and Civil Surgeon for epidemic management and prevention of infectious diseases.
article.articleSummary: On 4 November 2026, Chhattisgarh’s health department issued nine-point directives to CMHOs and Civil Surgeons to manage epidemics amid potential floods and cyclones. District and block-level 24x7 Health Control Rooms will be established; Rapid Response Teams (RRTs) will be ready to investigate outbreaks, identify cases and contacts, trace sources, provide treatment and referrals. Regular surveillance of diarrhoea, fever, jaundice, vomiting, and other infectious diseases will be reviewed daily; reporting via IDSP-IHIP portals (S, P, L forms) with lab confirmation as needed. Ensure ample stocks of ORS, zinc, IV fluids, anti-venom, chlorine tablets, PPE, masks, gloves, and testing supplies, kept in air-tight containers. Water safety and vector control are prioritized: chlorination, monitoring drinking water in relief camps, and elimination of mosquito breeding to curb dengue, malaria, and chikungunya. Relief camps will host health check-ups; mobile teams and ambulances will aid pregnant women, children, elderly, and disabled. CMHO reports to state DM Cell daily on affected villages, camps, cases, deaths, stock, water status, staffing, and referrals.

article.articleHeadline: Climate change and health: Doctor explains how extreme weather increases the risk of infections, respiratory problems and anxiety
article.articleSummary: Rising night-time temperatures and changing rainfall patterns in India are raising multiple health risks. Indians have lost about 64 hours of sleep annually between 2021 and 2025 due to higher night-time temperatures (Lancet Countdown). Dr Divya Gopal, additional director of internal medicine at Sir HN Reliance Foundation Hospital in Mumbai, notes that heat stress worsens cardiovascular and renal function, reduces blood flow, and disrupts sleep, with spillover into mental well-being. Climate-driven air pollution and irritants aggravate respiratory conditions such as asthma and COPD. Changing patterns of vector-borne diseases—dengue, malaria and chikungunya—along with floods that contaminate drinking water, raise diarrhoea, gastroenteritis and cholera risks. Food security and nutrition may be affected, increasing malnutrition risks among children and pregnant women; mental health impacts include anxiety and depression, especially for outdoor workers. India needs sustained surveillance, heat-health action plans, early warning systems, urban planning, and strengthened healthcare, beyond seasonal framing.

article.articleHeadline: How community-led AI-powered X-Rays are helping find TB among those without symptoms
article.articleSummary: AI-powered chest X-ray screening at two government ART centers in Delhi diagnosed 21 active TB cases among 1,559 people screened, of whom 12 were asymptomatic. The initiative, embedded in community-based efforts such as HIV care follow-ups and mobile screening camps, shows that X-ray screening can detect TB that verbal screening would miss. For people living with HIV, early TB detection and linkage to treatment are critical, since TB remains the most common opportunistic infection and the leading cause of death in this group. The findings were presented at NATCON 2026 in Patiala, India, highlighting the ongoing challenge that those needing screening are not always the ones who appear sick.

article.articleHeadline: The HIV injection, which reduces the risk of infection by 99.9%, is now available.
article.articleSummary: lenacavapir, an injectable HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis agent, received FDA approval in the United States and is expected to expand global access by making a cheaper generic version available from Dr. Reddy's Laboratories (India) and Unitaid. The injectable reduces the risk of HIV transmission by 99.9% compared with unprotected exposure, with dosing every six months, replacing daily oral PrEP regimens. The branded product previously cost over $14,000 per dose, limiting uptake; the generic will be available at about $20 per dose. With FDA clearance, regulators in many countries are likely to accelerate approvals, making this injectable accessible in roughly 120 low- and middle-income countries, potentially within weeks in some places. WHO estimates: in 2025, about 41 million people living with HIV worldwide and 570,000 HIV-related deaths. The generic rollout could reach about 20 million people at risk.

article.articleHeadline: Why did thousands of chickens die in Cuddalore in a single week?
article.articleSummary: Six coastal poultry farms in Cuddalore district, Tamil Nadu, have reported thousands of chicken deaths over the past week around the Diwali period. Farmers claim more than 9,000 birds died across six farms; one farmer says about 4,000 of 5,000 on his farm died in a week, with district losses potentially around 30,000. Government investigators collected carcasses and sent samples to laboratories in Chennai and Namakkal; results are expected in 2–3 days. Tests have ruled out low-virulence avian influenza, while authorities are testing for toxins or other causes. Seasonal factors such as heat stress and rising humidity on coastal farms are considered. Officials have advised reporting any unusual symptoms or sudden deaths and have restricted bringing new chicks pending results; compensation decisions will follow the investigations.

article.articleHeadline: Toxic water flowing in the Pavitra Hansla River; lab report reveals it; dangerous bacteria found ten times above the standard.
article.articleSummary: Untreated sewage from a 5 MLD Sewage Treatment Plant has polluted the Hansla River (Sarhind Drain) in Fatehgarh Sahib, Punjab. PPCB lab results, obtained via RTI, show alarming pollution: BOD 15 mg/L (NGT standard <10), Total Suspended Solids 24 mg/L (standard <20), fecal coliform 2100 MPN (standard 230). The district administration had claimed the plant was in ‘under testing/stabilization mode’ and that treated water would be diverted to soil-conservation irrigation, but the PPCB outlet sample contradicts this, with the river receiving contaminated effluent. The National Green Tribunal is hearing a related case, with government agencies yet to submit responses. Health and ecological risks are severe: high BOD depletes dissolved oxygen, fecal bacteria rise, and exposure can lead to cholera, typhoid, hepatitis, and skin infections; irrigation of crops could introduce toxins and bacteria into the food chain, potentially causing cancer and liver diseases. The case underscores administrative inaction and ongoing environmental hazard as of 2026.

article.articleHeadline: Red alert in the capital: Dhanmondi, DU, and DMCH top high-risk dengue list
article.articleSummary: Dengue fever threat intensifies in Dhaka after a 12-day monsoon larval survey (Sept 27–Oct 8) by DSCC across 75 wards. Aedes larvae/pupae were found in 322 of 2,250 inspected premises. The highest risk hotspots are Ward 15 (Dhanmondi), Ward 20 (DMCH), and Ward 21 (Dhaka University), with Ward 16 (Bagan) and Wards 18–19 (Kakrail) among other elevated areas. Overall, 29 wards are high risk, 28 moderate, and 18 under standard monitoring. Zones span Khilgaon, Basabo-Fakirapul, Shahjahanpur, Malibagh, Rajarbagh, Hazaribagh, Lalbagh, Azimpur, Bakshibazar, Jhaurchar, West Rasulpur, Moulvibazar, West Jurain, Alambagh, plus North Kutubkhali and Adarshabag. Breteau, House, Container, and Pupa indices guided risk. Primary breeding grounds include plastic buckets (14.21%), drums (11.22%), stagnant basement water (9.98%), and plastic mugs (9.92%), with detached homes and multi-storey units most affected. DSCC uses red/yellow/green mapping, weekly fogging by 12 joint teams, and enforcement to curb spread.

article.articleSummary: Twenty new leprosy cases were detected in Kolhapur district during a special survey conducted Sept 16–Oct 31, 2026. Dr. Hemlata Palekar, assistant director of health services (leprosy), said the goal is to reduce spread to zero by 2027 and urged people with symptoms to visit a government hospital for early diagnosis and treatment.

article.articleHeadline: Temasek Life Sciences Laboratory launches regional One Health initiative to strengthen early warning against infectious disease threats

article.articleHeadline: Understanding DT and Td Immunizations to Protect Children from Diphtheria and Tetanus
article.articleSummary: Indonesia's School Immunization Month (BIAS) DT and Td vaccines aim to sustain protection as children grow. DT is given to elementary grade 1 students (typically 7 years old) as an early booster against diphtheria and tetanus; Td, the follow-on booster replacing TT, is administered to students in grade 2 and grade 5 (or ages 8 and 11 for non-scholars) each November, extending protection into adolescence and beyond. Antibody titers wane after infancy, so these boosters raise protection above 90%, helping prevent diphtheria (Corynebacterium diphtheriae) and tetanus (Clostridium tetani) and their dangerous complications—diphtheria can cause severe throat pain with a grey-white pseudomembrane and possible heart and kidney failure; tetanus causes severe muscle spasms and breathing difficulties. Success depends on collaboration among health, education, religious, and local authorities, schools, and parents who complete health screening, ensure meals before vaccination, and monitor post-immunization, strengthening herd immunity in Indonesia.

article.articleHeadline: A mother with influenza A: how can she prevent transmitting the disease to newborns?
article.articleSummary: Influenza A in a breastfeeding mother does not transmit via breast milk; mothers may continue nursing if well, with precautions to prevent respiratory spread. Flu A spreads through respiratory droplets, so close contact with the infant poses exposure risk. Pumping milk is acceptable; when possible, a healthy family member should feed the baby using expressed milk. Key measures: thorough handwashing before touching the infant; wearing a well-fitted mask during feeding or near the baby; avoid kissing the infant’s face or hands while symptomatic; ensure a ventilated room and clean pumping equipment. If possible, another caregiver handles diapering and soothing. Infants under 6 months cannot be vaccinated; household members should receive annual influenza vaccination. Seek early medical care for mother (two weeks postpartum higher risk) or infant if warning signs appear; oseltamivir may be used with low transfer into breast milk.

article.articleHeadline: Just back from the street, holding my child, with a runny nose, still cuddling the baby: Habits that easily spread RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) to children
article.articleSummary: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) infection remains common in Vietnam, with Hanoi reporting seasonal peaks in March–April and September–November. RSV causes bronchiolitis and pneumonia in children under 2 years, especially those under 6 months. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets and contact with contaminated surfaces; adults and older children may have mild cough or runny nose, facilitating household spread. Alarm signs in infants include poor feeding with rapid breathing, chest retractions, or fatigue; blue lips, apnea, or lethargy require emergency care. Prevention centers on hand hygiene, surface cleaning, masking around babies, limiting exposure to crowds, and ensuring ventilation. WHO-recommended preventive options are maternal RSV vaccination in late pregnancy and postnatal long-acting monoclonal antibodies. Guidance from Hanoi Children’s Hospital, Hung Vuong Hospital, and the WHO covers risk groups and vaccination/antibody strategies for RSV prevention.

article.articleHeadline: Điện Biên is ready with a plan to respond to natural disasters, disease outbreaks, and security crises.
article.articleSummary: On November 4, 2026, Dien Bien Province issued a framework and response plans for a Level-2 multi-crisis scenario, prioritizing protection of life and health, disease control, misinformation management, and public order. The exercise imagines simultaneous hazards: protracted rainstorms causing floods, landslides, and isolation of villages; outbreaks of infectious diseases; and misinformation-driven unrest with price volatility in essential goods. The response emphasizes maintaining electricity, water, and health services while preventing crises from spreading. The three-stage process covers information intake, initial handling, and risk assessment, followed by emergency action under the '4-at-site' principle, relief, infrastructure repair, production recovery, and social welfare. Commune-level forces organize evacuations and shelters; the provincial police assess risk, advise activation, and coordinate rescue, traffic restoration, disease control, and online misinformation countermeasures. The provincial People's Committee assigns the police as the standing body to lead drills and ensure inter-agency coordination to avoid paralysis in complex, concurrent events.

article.articleHeadline: Rescuing a 17-day-old neonate with dengue shock and severe liver injury.
article.articleSummary: On 2026-11-04, a 17-day-old male neonate from Tan Vinh Loc, Ho Chi Minh City, was treated at Ho Chi Minh City Children’s Hospital for dengue shock syndrome with severe liver injury. He presented after two days of fever with lethargy, irritability, a generalized rash and petechiae, and shock (blood pressure 60/40 mmHg). Laboratory results showed hematocrit 45%, platelets 24,000/mm3, AST 1369 U/L, and ALT 245 U/L. Diagnosed with dengue shock syndrome with severe hepatic injury, he received aggressive resuscitation: 6% Volulyte fluids, transfusion of packed red cells and platelets, albumin, liver support, and respiratory support including oxygen and CPAP. After 72 hours, hemodynamic status and liver injury improved; no further bleeding; he was awake and feeding well. Neonatal dengue can present non-specifically, requiring careful neonatal specialty assessment and tailored treatment to optimize outcomes.

article.articleHeadline: RSV cases surge 30%; not just a children's disease—elderly at risk of severe pneumonia
article.articleSummary: Thailand reports 5,683 RSV cases from Jan 1 to Aug 15, 2026 (8.63 per 100,000), up 30% from the same period in 2025. Disease affects all ages, with 0–4-year-olds having the highest incidence, but elderly (≥60 years) and those with chronic conditions are at risk of severe disease. About 40% of patients require hospitalization; risk factors include age, chronic lung/heart/kidney disease, and immunocompromise. RSV can cause lower respiratory tract infections such as bronchiolitis and pneumonia, presenting initially with fever, cough, and runny nose, potentially leading to dyspnea and hypoxemia; some cases need ICU care or ventilation. There is no RSV-specific antiviral; treatment is supportive. Preventive measures include hand hygiene, masks, and avoiding close contact with the sick. For those aged 50+ or with comorbidities, consult a physician about RSV vaccination (adjuvanted or non-adjuvanted), effective against RSV A and B. Vaccination confusion with pneumococcal vaccines is noted. RSV Awareness Week 2026 highlights these risks in Thailand.

article.articleHeadline: NS1-based IgG ELISA with OD ratio improves ZIKV and dengue serology in
article.articleSummary: Thailand researchers evaluated an in-house NS1-based IgG ELISA to distinguish past ZIKV infections from past DENV infections in a dengue-endemic setting. Using RT-PCR–confirmed ZIKV or DENV samples, they compared three ZIKV antigens—envelope protein domain III and NS1 from African-lineage MR766 and Asian-lineage SV0127—and applied three ZIKV/DENV ratio metrics (positive-to-negative, optical density, and relative optical density). The Asian SV0127 NS1 antigen with the relative OD ratio yielded the best discrimination. Validation with a Youden index cut-off of 2.35 produced an AUC of 0.7083 (95% CI 0.6335–0.7831), sensitivity 58.3%, and specificity 79.2%. Compared with a commercial Zika IgG ELISA, the in-house NS1-based assay demonstrated better discrimination despite lower overall signal. The approach aims for surveillance and retrospective serology in settings where neutralization tests are impractical and is not a replacement for PRNT.

article.articleHeadline: Suspected patients test negative for Ebola after returning to Israel from DRC, Health Ministry says
article.articleSummary: Two suspected Ebola patients returning from the Democratic Republic of the Congo were placed in isolation at Sheba Medical Center and Ichilov Medical Center in Israel, and both tested negative for Ebola. Israel's Health Ministry said there are no confirmed Ebola cases in the country. The DRC Ebola outbreak has infected over 10,000 people and killed more than 5,000 since it was first declared in May. The outbreak has spread to Uganda, Kenya, and Nigeria, prompting travel advisories by the Health Ministry, urging avoidance of nonessential travel to several countries including South Sudan, the Central African Republic, Rwanda, Burundi, Tanzania, Zambia, and Angola. The outbreak is caused by the Ebola Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no vaccine or cure. Transmission occurs via close contact with symptomatic patients or bodily fluids, contaminated objects, or infected animals.

article.articleHeadline: Zambia will invest 213 million dollars in a cholera vaccine factory.
article.articleSummary: Zambia will invest 213 million dollars in ZAMVAX, a cholera vaccine factory to be built in the Lusaka-South Economic Zone. An agreement signed on November 2 outlines a two-phase project aiming to boost local production and regional supply. Phase 1, valued at about 24.13 million dollars, will establish an oral cholera vaccine packaging unit with annual capacity up to 20 million doses, with production split evenly between domestic use and exports. Phase 2 aims to locally manufacture vaccine active ingredients to reduce import dependence. In the long term, the facility could expand to pediatric and veterinary vaccines, strengthening Zambia’s health autonomy and contributing to regional vaccination capacity. The plan indicates emphasis on self-sufficiency and broader supply chains for cholera vaccines in the region.
